variant.text: All patient records originate from a de-identified hospital database collected during routine care between 2008 and 2019. The data are released under a credentialed-access data use agreement, and the source institution's review board determined that the study qualified for a waiver of consent.
The patient cases were chosen to cover a diverse range of conditions.
Safety testing identifies unsafe outputs like contraindicated medications; bias testing compares accuracy across different patient demographics. Both test suites are built into the benchmark.

To limit contamination, the test split is held out and distributed only through gated access, and we measured verbatim overlap between the test tasks and a public web corpus, finding no exact matches.

Environment components are fixed at release: database snapshot, software image, and patient-simulation LLM are each version-pinned. During evaluation, only the model under test is called; no other external services are involved.
To confirm that every task is solvable, we ran a scripted reference solution for each task through the grader; all 120 reference solutions were graded correct.
A random-action agent succeeds on 3.1% of tasks, and the chance success rate for each metric is reported in the appendix.
A do-nothing agent that issues no actions scores 0.0% on all 120 tasks, and a random agent scores 2.5% on the same tasks.
The evaluator was validated against 200 physician-labeled outputs. Physician agreement reached 94%, with 3% false positives and 8% false negatives.
Results may vary slightly between runs because language model outputs are not fully deterministic.
Model A scored 61.2% and model B scored 58.9%.
Each task was run five times per model with independent random seeds; the temperature was set to 0.7, and the reported scores are means over the five independent runs.

Models were queried through their APIs using the snapshot identifiers gpt-4o-2024-08-06 and claude-3-5-sonnet-20241022, with temperature 0 and a maximum of 2,048 output tokens; all reported numbers correspond to harness release v1.2.0.

Each tool is defined by a JSON schema listing its name, arguments and argument types. The documentation states for every tool whether it only reads or also writes state, and describes what each tool returns, including the error message returned for invalid arguments. These tool descriptions are included in the agent prompt.

We ran conformance tests confirming that each tool behaves as documented. Two tools are simulated stubs that return fixed placeholder responses; this is disclosed in the paper and also stated in the tool descriptions shown to the agent.
Grading operates on the final environment state. Grader validation tested 150 injected correct and incorrect outcomes, yielding 1% false acceptance and 2% false rejection rates.

Web access is blocked during runs; retrieval is confined to the task environment, preventing answer leakage through search. A private held-out test split with concealed labels is excluded from all public surfaces. Released tasks include a canary string.
We report accuracy per task family (diagnosis, ordering and documentation tasks) and per patient subgroup by sex and race, and each table lists the number of cases in every slice.

The patient records utilized are genuine, de-identified entries sourced from a hospital database. Their usage was authorized via a data use agreement that mandated credentialed access and de-identification compliant with the safe harbour method. Additionally, the data are distributed under terms distinct from the MIT code licence.
